40F here to establish. Moved her care from a practice in the Pioneer Valley she'd been at for years; wanted someone she could actually reach. Records requested.

PMH:
- Parkinson disease, young onset. Dx 2017 by outside neurology, who still follows her and writes the carbidopa-levodopa. Says it works well, she rarely notices anything on her doses. Sees them roughly yearly.
- Iron deficiency anemia, put down to heavy periods. Periods regular, heavy, the first two days especially. Has been on OTC ferrous sulfate for years, takes it with a vitamin C tab. Never had IV iron. No GYN workup she can recall.
- Nosebleeds since she was a teenager, a few a month, worse in winter. Cauterized once at 25. Father has the same and was told he had AVMs in his lungs. A paternal aunt also bleeds from the nose.
- Allergic rhinitis, tree pollen and dust. Loratadine when needed.

PSH: nasal cautery age 25.
Meds: carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 1 tab TID; ferrous sulfate 325 daily w/ vit C; loratadine 10 prn.
Allergies: NKDA. Shellfish -> itching and hives. Tree pollen, dust mites.
FHx: father nosebleeds + lung AVMs; paternal aunt nosebleeds; mother hypothyroid, generalized anxiety; son (12) has ADHD.
SH: teaches high school math. Married; lives in Sunderland with husband and her son (son is from her first marriage, his dad lives out of state). Vegetarian. Never smoked. 1-2 glasses of wine a week. PHQ-2 0.

ROS: tired by late afternoon most days, which she has gotten used to. No chest pain, no melena or hematochezia, no syncope.

Exam: well appearing, slightly pale conjunctivae. HEENT otherwise unremarkable. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abd soft, NT. No edema. Neuro: no tremor at rest today, gait normal, speech normal.

A/P:
1. Iron deficiency anemia, chronic. CBC, iron studies today. Continue ferrous sulfate. Will discuss GYN once I see where she is.
2. Parkinson disease - per neurology. Will ask for their notes.
3. Recurrent epistaxis with a strong family story - noted.
4. Allergic rhinitis - loratadine prn.
5. HM: CMP, lipids, TSH; HCV and HIV screening (consented). Due for first mammogram - ordered. Pap/HPV per old records.
RTC for annual next fall, sooner prn.

conditions.note: Curacao criteria: epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias, affected first-degree relative

reports.text: Indication: exertional dyspnea, suspected hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia; evaluate for intrapulmonary shunt. Technically adequate study. Normal left ventricular size and wall thickness. Left ventricular ejection fraction 72% by biplane method, high normal, with no regional wall motion abnormality. Normal right ventricular size and function. Atria normal in size. Aortic, mitral, tricuspid and pulmonic valves structurally normal without stenosis or regurgitation. Estimated right ventricular systolic pressure normal. No pericardial effusion. Agitated saline injected via left antecubital vein at rest and with Valsalva release: no bubbles seen in the left heart at any cycle.
reports.conclusion: High-normal LV systolic function (EF 72%). No valvular abnormality. Agitated saline contrast study negative for intracardiac or intrapulmonary shunt.

documents.title: Pulmonology Consultation
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
Re: Paula Wisniewski, DOB 3/9/1979. Seen 3/17/2021 at your request.

Reason: worsening exertional dyspnea and nosebleeds.

History: 42-year-old teacher, never smoker, with nosebleeds dating back to her early teens, cauterized once in her twenties, now more frequent. Over the winter she has become breathless climbing stairs. No cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, migraine-type headaches or neurologic events. Her father carries a diagnosis of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia with treated pulmonary AVMs, and a paternal aunt has the same nosebleed history. Her husband's side has nothing similar. She and her husband are concerned about her son, now 13, and whether he could have inherited this.

Medications: carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 TID (neurology), ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily with vitamin C, loratadine as needed.
Allergies: no drug allergies; shellfish (hives); environmental.

Examination: comfortable at rest, SpO2 98% on room air. Several small red telangiectasias on the lower lip and tongue tip and on the pads of two fingers on the right hand, blanching. Nasal septum with crusting. Lungs clear; no bruit over the chest. Heart regular, no murmur. No clubbing or cyanosis.

Data: labs from your office and ours show iron deficiency anemia, hemoglobin in the 9s with microcytosis. Transthoracic echo with bubble study today: EF 72%, valves normal, no shunt.

Assessment: she meets three of the four Curacao criteria (spontaneous recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias at characteristic sites, a first-degree relative with HHT), which makes the diagnosis of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia definite. I explained that HHT is autosomal dominant and arises from defects in the TGF-beta signaling pathway in blood vessel walls, so each of her children has a 50% chance of inheriting it. The negative bubble study makes a clinically significant pulmonary AVM unlikely, and I attribute her exertional dyspnea to the iron deficiency anemia, which in turn is fed by both her heavy menses and the nosebleeds.

Recommendations: continue iron replacement through your office; nasal humidification as you started. Return to us for new respiratory symptoms.

Thank you for the referral.
Pulmonology

documents.title: Neurology Follow-up Letter
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
Re: Paula Wisniewski, DOB 03/09/1979. Seen 03/14/2022.

Paula, 43, whom we follow for Parkinson disease and who was diagnosed with HHT by pulmonology last year, came back to clinic, a little overdue for her annual visit, mainly because of poor sleep.

For roughly the past year, once she lies down at night she gets a deep, unpleasant ache in both calves with an overwhelming need to move her legs. Getting up and walking eases it, and she often paces her bedroom several times before she can fall asleep. It happens only in the evening and at night when she is still; standing, sitting through the school day and daytime are free of it. She is tired every day from the lost sleep. She has no history of anxiety, depression or any other psychiatric problem. Parkinson symptoms remain well controlled on carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 three times daily.

She eats a vegetarian diet. Menses are regular but heavy. She remains on oral iron for long-standing iron deficiency.

Examination on medication: neurologic examination normal, including mental status, cranial nerves, strength, tone, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait. No tremor or bradykinesia.

Impression:
1. Restless legs syndrome, meeting all essential criteria, with chronic insomnia as its consequence. Iron deficiency is the most likely driver here.
2. Parkinson disease, stable.

We discussed management. The first step is iron: her ferritin should be checked, and the goal in RLS is a ferritin above 75, well above the usual lower limit. Please check iron studies and consider whether she can reach that orally. Regular sleep and wake times, moderate exercise earlier in the day, cutting back on evening wine and caffeine, and avoiding sedating antihistamines such as diphenhydramine at night (her loratadine is fine). We also talked about what this means long term: RLS is usually chronic and can slowly become more frequent, and dopaminergic medicines used for it can over time worsen it (augmentation), which is one reason we are not adding anything today. No change to her carbidopa-levodopa.

Follow-up in 12 months.

documents.title: Psychiatry Consultation
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
Re: Paula Wisniewski, DOB 03/09/1979. Outpatient psychiatric evaluation 07/01/2024. Referred by her primary care physician.

Identifying data: 45-year-old married high school math teacher with HHT, Parkinson disease, iron deficiency anemia and restless legs, seen four months after GI evaluated her for dysphagia and a sore tongue related to iron deficiency.

Chief concern: increasing trouble speaking over three months.

HPI: In early April she had a heated argument with her teenage son and told him she wished she had never raised him. He left two days later to stay with his father in another state, and they have had little contact since. Her voice became strained right after the argument and she has since lost the ability to project it; she whispers or writes notes. No sore throat, cough or recent respiratory illness. She describes a persistent sadness and intense guilt over what she said and keeps returning to the moment. Sleep is broken: it takes her a long time to fall asleep and she wakes often, sometimes replaying the argument. She finished the term at school but avoided the phone and stopped speaking up in staff meetings, and colleagues commented that she seemed withdrawn. She still enjoys her usual activities but has been socializing less because of her voice. No flashbacks, intrusive images or nightmares about the event. No hallucinations or delusions at any time. No meaningful change in weight or appetite. Since April she also describes near-constant worry that she finds hard to switch off, with muscle tension. No fever, neck lumps or swallowing problems now.

Psychiatric history: none prior. No previous treatment. Family: mother with generalized anxiety disorder and hypothyroidism.
Substances: wine occasionally; never smoked; no drugs.
Safety: denies suicidal or homicidal ideation; future oriented; supportive husband.

Mental status: well groomed, cooperative. Speech is a whisper with normal articulation and language; she can cough normally. Mood "guilty." Affect constricted, visibly anxious when the argument is discussed. Thought process linear; no psychotic content. Cognition grossly intact. Insight and judgment good.
Brief exam: oropharynx normal; cranial nerves intact.
GAD-7: 13.

Assessment:
1. Functional neurological disorder with speech symptoms (functional aphonia), onset after an acute interpersonal stressor, with a normal oropharynx, intact cranial nerves and a preserved cough.
2. Generalized anxiety disorder.
No PTSD, no psychotic features.

Plan:
- Explained the diagnosis as a real, reversible problem with how the voice is being controlled, not damage to the voice box.
- Referral to speech therapy for voice retraining.
- Weekly CBT-based psychotherapy here, focused on the guilt and worry, sleep and reconnecting with her son.
- No medication at this time; she prefers therapy first.
- Follow-up in about 3 months.

Thank you for this referral.

BP 125/80, HR 88, RR 16, afebrile. No wheeze, no stridor, no lip or tongue swelling. Transfusion stopped immediately; line kept open with saline. Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV. Blood bank notified, transfusion reaction workup sent.
12:10 Hives fading, itch resolved.
Transfusion reaction workup: clerical and ABO/Rh recheck concordant; direct antiglobulin test negative; post-reaction plasma without visible hemolysis; urinalysis negative for blood. No evidence of an acute hemolytic reaction. Blood bank: mild allergic (urticarial) reaction.
16:30 After diphenhydramine 25 mg IV premedication, a new unit started slowly; completed 19:15 without any reaction.
21:10 Post-transfusion Hgb 7.7. No recurrent bleeding.

Impression:
1. Epistaxis from HHT, controlled.
2. Symptomatic iron deficiency anemia, transfused 1 unit PRBC.
3. Allergic (urticarial) transfusion reaction; acute hemolytic transfusion reaction excluded.

Disposition: home 21:50 with husband. Blood bank note added: premedicate with an antihistamine for future transfusions. PCP follow-up within 2-3 days; ENT and hematology referrals already placed by PCP, keep those. Return for bleeding not controlled with 20 minutes of pressure, fainting, chest pain, rash or breathing trouble.

Re: Paula Wisniewski, DOB 03/09/1979. Seen 12/09/2025.

HHT with nosebleeds since adolescence, cauterized once at 25, near-daily since October with an ED visit and transfusion on 11/3. Now 2-3 short bleeds a week after IV iron and humidification.

Exam: anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy show multiple small telangiectasias over the anterior septum on both sides, more on the right, with a fresh crust on the right. No septal perforation. Posterior nasal cavity and nasopharynx unremarkable. Oral cavity with a few small telangiectasias on the lip and tongue tip.

Assessment: HHT-related epistaxis from anterior septal telangiectasias.
Plan: continue nightly saline gel and bedroom humidification; avoid nose blowing hard and nasal steroid sprays. In-office laser coagulation of the anterior septal telangiectasias under topical anesthesia, scheduled 1/13/2026. Avoid chemical or electrocautery and non-absorbable packing.

documents.title: Nasal Laser Coagulation
documents.author: ENT
documents.body:
Procedure: laser coagulation of anterior septal telangiectasias, bilateral, in office.
Indication: HHT epistaxis.
Anesthesia: topical lidocaine with oxymetazoline pledgets.
Findings: multiple small telangiectasias of the anterior septum bilaterally, right more than left, as at consultation.
Technique: under endoscopic guidance, lesions treated with low-power laser in a circumferential pattern from the periphery inward, avoiding the central vessel. Minimal bleeding, controlled with a pledget. No packing.
Patient tolerated well. Instructions: saline gel three times daily for two weeks, humidifier, no nose blowing for a week, expect crusting. Follow-up 6 weeks.
